questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
- The possibility of receiving an Erasmus grant
- An interesting course catalogue
- It was an English-speaking country
- The possibility of going on trips in the highlands
- An interesting and beautiful city
- The university's good academic reputation and ratings

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was a bit confusing at times, because we received a lot of different emails with a lot of information from different senders. It was possible, however, to find most of the information needed, either by looking through the emails or by contacting the study abroad advisors.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was assigned a study abroad advisor who I could turn to for help.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: We spent quite a lot of time searching on different sites such as SpareRoom, Airbnb or different Facebook groups, including The Meadows Share. We eventually found our housing through a site called Edlets and were very happy about it.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
It can be quite hard finding something in Edinburgh, so it's a good idea to start looking at least 2 months before your stay. There are some good options at
Edlets.com
(might look a bit sketchy, but we had a completely fine experience using them - they were service-minded and easy to get in touch with).
Maybe make a videocall with the landlord to make sure it is not scam. Also make sure to get a decent contract with clear agreements about insurance, deposits etc. Our landlord at first asked us to transfer all the money (for the full rental period) before arrival, but because we did not feel safe doing so, we made an agreement to meet at the apartment on the first day and then transferred the money to him.
I personally enjoyed having "my own" place, but I think living in student accommodation/on campus housing is definitely a great way to meet new people.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Sometimes the course catalogue and the course registration site was not fully aligned which created some confusion and frustration.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: When applying for the university (in May), you have to make a list of the courses you would like (but this is only to give the university an idea of which courses you would like, it's not a final choice). You can read about most of the available courses on the online 'course finder'. The official registration process begins in July where you apply for the courses that you want through an application form. When a decision has been made, you receive an email from the university. If you do not get enrolled in the courses that you applied for, you have to make a new course application. If you want to make changes, it can be done either through a new application form or by sending an email to the visiting students office, depending on which college you belong to. You can change courses until week 2 of the semester.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
The visiting students offices at the University of Edinburgh were available and quite helpful.
Also, the university has a website which can help you create an overview of the courses that you are interested in, to make sure the course schedules do not overlap.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got most of the courses that I registered for. However, I was a bit disappointed that some of the courses that I had found through the course finder were not available to me (as an exchange student) in the actual registration process.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Checking out the course catalogue when choosing your exchange destination is important. You should make sure there are a lot of different courses that you would be interested in taking and keep an open mind throughout the process, because the course catalogue may change, even shortly before semester start. At the University of Edinburgh, it is possible to change courses within the first two weeks of the semester.
Also make sure to check out the schedule (if possible) to make sure the lectures don't overlap.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took both 1st and 4th year courses, so the level naturally differed quite a lot. However, I think the reading and the subjects that we explored were generally on a high level, and the lecturers seemed very competent. Sometimes I found the discussions between students a bit disappointing compared to what I am used to, but that might have something to do with the age difference (generally undergraduates from other countries are younger than the Danish students).

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The ratio between lectures and self-study was different. At UCPH I am used to having 20-25 hours of lectures/tutorials, while in Edinburgh I only had 8 hours weekly (but a larger amount of reading).
The in-class teaching style and the student-lecturer relationship was similar in many ways. However, I experienced a larger focus on the students' learning process/experience (e.g., by asking the students to write 'reflective course diaries' which were part of the final assessments/exams).
Furthermore, the autumn semester at Edinburgh is very short (only 11 weeks), which made it quite intensive. Sometimes it felt like there was not enough time to process the things we learned about.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
A) Conservation Science (ECSC10036)
B) Environmentalism: Past and Present (STIS08010)
C) Sustainable Development 1a: Introducing Sustainable Development (SCIL08008)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend all the courses, but for different reasons.
Course B (2nd year course) and C (1st year course) had a broader academic approach and welcomed students from many different fields of study, which made it easy to participate as an "outsider" at your host university.
Course A (a 4th year course) was more narrow and there were higher/more specific requirements for the students' academic background (it required some fundamental knowledge of ecology). 
The workload and level was higher on course A and B.
To me, it was nice to have courses with different levels of ambition, but I guess it depends on how much you wish to delve into your studies vs. prioritize other things (social events, trips, etc.) on your exchange stay.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Groceries were cheaper than expected (tip: If you live nearby one of the bigger Sainsbury's, make sure to get a Nectar card - it's free and gives you some good discounts!). Coffee and beer prices were also cheaper than in Denmark.
I was also happy to find out that all teaching materials were freely available online, so we were not required to buy any books.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were a lot of clubs to join, especially sports clubs. The university also has a gym (called Pleasance) with great facilities, and the membership fee is not too pricey (around 650 DKK for the whole semester). There were also various social events for Erasmus and other visiting students, especially in the welcome week.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would definitely recommend joining the gym - it's a great opportunity to get some physical activity into your everyday. Plus the gym has a sauna, which is really nice on the cold and wet autumn days.
I would also definitely recommend going to a ceilidh (traditional Scottish folk dance) at Stramash, it's a lot of fun and a nice way to experience some local culture.
Another nice thing to know is that most museums in Edinburgh have free entrance.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Explore the different areas of the city, and go on trips to see some of the beautiful Scottish highlands. I really enjoyed going on trips, including:
- Day trips to Pentland Hills south of Edinburgh
- Hiking to and sleeping in a bothy (we went to Over Phawhope Bothy).
- Hiking some of West Highland Way
- Car trip to Isle of Skye
- Day trip to Pitlochry, including a hike to Ben Vrackie
- Visiting some smaller Scottish towns, including Stirling and Oban

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy, the Scottish culture is not that different from the Danish.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It can be hard to get to know locals, but I believe talking to people in classes and maybe at pubs is the best way to do it.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Nothing in particular.
I was sometimes surprised that the cafes in Edinburgh close quite early compared to Denmark, but that wasn't exactly a challenge.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The pub culture is great - it is a more informal way of going out compared to Denmark, which makes it easier to do on an everyday. The pub atmosphere is really nice and cosy and it is a great place to hang out, whether you want to go for a coffee, a pint of beer, or some food.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Make sure to go on trips into the highlands (and maybe plan a bit ahead, the semester is so short).
2) Be prepared to spend a lot of time on your studies, especially in the last part of the semester. You often have to write your midterms and final exams while you still have classes/lectures, which can be stressful. But try not to let it take up all of your time and energy in your last weeks there.
3) If you have the opportunity, I would recommend arriving a week or at least some days before the welcome week. It's nice to have some days to get settled in your accommodation, get a little familiar with your new area, and to start exploring the city before the semester starts.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure to check you university emails daily before and upon arrival - there is a lot of important information and things you have to do in the beginning. And contact your student advisor if you have questions.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
One thing that I really enjoyed about being on exchange was how it offered me the chance to have a different everyday life, with less plans and commitments than what I was used to. Naturally, I still had to spend a lot of time studying, but it was a nice sort of "break" from a busy life at home. At the same time, it also makes you realize and appreciate the things you miss at home.
Other than that, I have really enjoyed the opportunity to go on trips and explore the beautiful Scottish nature. The trips are definitely some of the greatest experiences from my exchange stay.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Language was a surprisingly big challenge for me. Speaking English in informal everyday contexts is one thing, but academic English is challenging on another level. It was often a barrier for my participation in class, which was frustrating. However, my language skills also improved during the semester, which was a positive experience.

Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
